heading: Why History Is a Design Tool
original:
01
Conventions exist for reasons
The crown at 3 o'clock, the 12/6/9 hierarchy, the swept seconds hand — each emerged from a specific functional or manufacturing constraint. When you break a convention, you must replace it with something better.
02
Collectors are your market
Serious buyers are historically literate. A design that accidentally echoes a celebrated reference gains depth. One that poorly imitates it loses credibility. You cannot navigate this without knowing the references.
03
Ideas repeat across eras
Sports-luxury crossover, oversized cases, two-tone metal, integrated bracelets — these have all appeared, disappeared, and returned. Understanding cycles gives you a better read on where design is going.
"The 1960s and 70s were incredibly creative and daring decades. What have we done since?"
— Emmanuel Gueit, designer of the Royal Oak Offshore

heading: The Escapement
original:
The single most important component in a watch — and the designer's constraint
01
Escape Wheel
Toothed wheel that releases one tooth per oscillation of the balance wheel. Transmits energy from gear train to balance. Typically 15–20 teeth.
02
Pallet Fork
The lever that controls the escape wheel. Pivots back and forth, catching and releasing the escape wheel teeth in alternation. The defining component of the Swiss lever escapement.
03
Impulse Pin
Small jewel on the balance roller that engages the pallet fork slot once per oscillation, ensuring the fork swings correctly and the balance receives an impulse of energy.
04
Balance Wheel
The oscillating wheel — the watch's pendulum. Its back-and-forth rotation at a fixed frequency (defined by hairspring tension and inertia) is what gives a watch its accuracy.
BEATS PER HOUR (BPH) — What it means for design
→  
18,000 BPH (5 Hz) — Vintage, languid tick. Lower wear on parts, longer service intervals.
→  
21,600 BPH (6 Hz) — Standard for most ETA-based movements. Smooth sweep.
→  
28,800 BPH (8 Hz) — Most common today. Smoother seconds hand. ETA 2824, Miyota 9015.
→  
36,000 BPH (10 Hz) — High-beat: Grand Seiko, Omega 8500. Exceptional accuracy. More wear.

original:
Birth of the Portable Timepiece
c.1510
Peter Henlein, Nuremberg
First spring-driven portable clock. Drum-shaped, worn around the neck. Accuracy: ±30 minutes/day. The concept of wearable timekeeping is born.
1657
Huygens — Pendulum Clock
Christiaan Huygens invents the pendulum clock, reducing daily error from ~15 minutes to ~15 seconds. Stationary timekeeping is transformed. The portable equivalent would come 18 years later.
1631
Worshipful Company of Clockmakers
London's clockmakers guild established — the first formal professional body in watchmaking. Thomas Tompion (1639–1713) and George Graham (1673–1751) later emerge from this tradition.
1675
Huygens — Balance Spring (Hairspring)
The invention that made portable accuracy possible. Published January 20, 1675 in the Journal des Sçavans. The coiled spring allows the balance wheel to oscillate at a regulated frequency. Still in use today. This is the fundamental innovation of portable horology.
1700
Case design begins to evolve
Early watches are purely functional objects in simple cases. As accuracy improves and watches become status symbols, the case begins to receive ornamental attention — enamel, engraving, precious metal.

heading: 1700 – 1850  —  The Age of Precision
original:
Abraham-Louis Breguet  (1747–1823)
The most cited reference point in watchmaking history. Invented or perfected: the tourbillon (1801), the over-coil hairspring (Breguet overcoil), the perpétuelle self-winding movement, the shock protection system (para-chute), and the guilloché engine-turned dial. His aesthetic — subtle, intellectual, deep — remains the template for high watchmaking.
1759
John Harrison H4
Marine chronometer solves longitude problem. Accuracy at sea = national security. Watchmaking funded by the British government.
1795–1801
Breguet Tourbillon
Conceived c.1793–1795 during Breguet's Swiss exile; patent filed and granted June 26, 1801. The rotating cage counteracts gravity's effect on pocket watch accuracy. First commercial sale: 1805.
1839
Patek Philippe founded
Geneva. The future home of the perpetual calendar and the world's most valuable auction watches. Founded on the principle of absolute precision.
1845
Waltham Mass. production
American factories begin producing interchangeable parts. Swiss craft vs American industry — a tension that defines the next 130 years.
Design legacy: Breguet's dial and hand aesthetic (the off-white, guilloché dial; the blued steel Breguet hands) is instantly identifiable 200 years later. This is what design longevity looks like.

heading: 1969–1983 — The Quartz Crisis
original:
1969
Seiko Astron — first quartz watch
Accurate to ±5 seconds/year. Revolutionary.
~50%
Swiss watch exports halved
From 1974 peak to early 1980s. An industry near collapse.
1,000+
Swiss watchmakers closed
Employment: 90,000 (1970) → 33,000 (1984) → 28,000 (1988).
What Happened
Japanese manufacturers (Seiko, Citizen) and then Hong Kong/Taiwanese producers offered quartz watches at a fraction of the cost and vastly superior accuracy. Swiss watchmakers, who had invested centuries in mechanical expertise, had no competitive answer. The mid-tier Swiss watch industry — watches priced between $50–$500 — was essentially destroyed.
The irony: The CEH (Centre Electronique Horloger) in Neuchâtel, Switzerland had developed quartz watch technology in parallel with Seiko and actually showed a prototype in 1967. But Swiss industry leaders failed to commercialise it aggressively, believing mechanical watches were too culturally embedded to be displaced.
The Salvation: Swatch (1983)
→  
Nicolas Hayek's insight: reclaim low-price quartz — but make it fashionable, Swiss, and disposable.
→  
Swatch used quartz to protect the Swiss industry's volume. Allowed Omega, Longines, IWC to reposition up the value chain.
→  
The mechanical watch became luxury, not commodity. This repositioning saved the industry and defined it for the next 40 years.

heading: 1984–Now — The Mechanical Renaissance & Independent Era
original:
1984–2000
Luxury Repositioning
Swiss brands abandon the mid-market. Rolex, Patek, AP become investment objects. IWC and Jaeger-LeCoultre revive heritage lines. Complications regain prestige.
2000–2010
Boom & Complexity
Pre-2008 boom. Ultra-complicated watches become status signifiers. Richard Mille founded 2001. Skeletonised movements, tonneau cases, avant-garde materials. The anti-dress-watch movement.
2010–2020
Microbrand Revolution
Internet lowers barriers to brand creation. Baltic, Lorier, AnOrdain, Halios, Farer emerge. Design-first brands with no Swiss heritage compete on taste, story, and value.
2020–Now
Consolidation & Craft
Premium segment booms post-COVID. Watch auctions hit new records. Secondary market explodes. But: overproduction in mid-tier, China slowdown 2024. Design quality bifurcates sharply.
Your opportunity as a designer: The microbrand category is the most open and design-forward segment of the entire watch market.

heading: Rolex
original:
Founded 1905 · Geneva · Private · ~1 million watches/year
Design Consistency
The Submariner dial has not changed fundamentally since 1953. The Datejust since 1945. This is not conservatism — it is brand equity protection. Every Rolex looks immediately like a Rolex. Students: what visual elements make this possible?
Material Innovation
Rolex develops proprietary materials: Oystersteel (904L stainless, harder and more corrosion-resistant than industry standard 316L), Cerachrom (ceramic bezel insert, scratch-proof), Chromalight (blue luminescent material). Innovation is functional, not aesthetic.
In-House Everything
Rolex is one of very few brands with end-to-end vertical integration: foundry, spring production, escapement, movement, case, bracelet, dial. This gives absolute control over quality and supply chain — and justifies the premium.
Brand as Investment
Rolex is the only watch brand with significant secondary market price support at retail price or above. The 'Rolex premium' is real and documented. This is the product of decades of supply control, quality consistency, and brand storytelling.
Key references to study: Submariner 124060 · Datejust 36 · GMT-Master II 'Pepsi' 126710 · Day-Date 40 · Explorer II 226570

heading: Patek Philippe  ·  Seiko
original:
Patek Philippe
Founded 1839  ·  Geneva  ·  Family owned
Positioning
The pinnacle of Swiss watchmaking. No marketing; word of mouth. Every purchase requires relationship with an AD.
Design language
Elegance through restraint. Calatrava: round, no-date, dome crystal. Nautilus: Genta's integrated bracelet, horizontal embossed dial. Both are icons of their category.
Complications
The perpetual calendar is Patek's signature complication. The 5711/5712 Nautilus are the most discussed modern pieces. The 5016A pocket watch: $7.3M at auction.
Brand positioning
"You never actually own a Patek Philippe. You merely look after it for the next generation." — This line is brand strategy, not tagline. It repositions the watch as patrimony.
Seiko
Founded 1881  ·  Tokyo  ·  Seiko Epson Group
Philosophy
Context-appropriate design. Functional beauty. The watch should be exactly what it claims to be — no more, no less.
Design language
Zaratsu-polished cases with hairline/mirror contrast. Snowflake hands (SKX/Presage). Grand Seiko Shizukuishi dials reflecting Japanese landscapes.
Innovation
Quartz (1969, Astron), Spring Drive (1999: quartz-regulated mechanical), Hi-Beat (36,000 BPH for accuracy). Led every major watch technology shift in 60 years.
Diversity
Five sub-brands: Grand Seiko (luxury), Seiko (mid), Seiko 5 (entry), Prospex (sport), Presage (craft). Each has distinct DNA and audience.

heading: What a Brand Actually Is
original:
A brand is NOT a logo
A logo is a symbol. A brand is the total perception someone has when they encounter that symbol. Rolex's crown logo has no intrinsic value — the associations accumulated over 100 years give it value.
A brand is NOT a product
Products are manufactured. Brands are felt. Two watches can share identical movements, cases, and dials — and be perceived entirely differently based on their brand context. The Omega Seamaster and a rebranded ETA 2824 watch are functionally similar. The perception gap is enormous.
A brand is NOT advertising
Advertising is what you say. Brand is what people believe. Patek Philippe spends almost nothing on advertising. They spend everything on product quality, distribution control, and reputation management. The result: the most desired watch brand on earth.
"A brand is a person's gut feeling about a product, service, or organisation."
— Marty Neumeier, The Brand Gap (2003)  ·  Free PDF: martyneumeier.com/the-brand-gap
Implication: You cannot control your brand. You can only influence it through consistent product quality, design, and communication over time.

heading: The Five Disciplines of Brand-Building
original:
01  Differentiate
Find the one thing that makes your brand unique and impossible to confuse with anyone else. In watches: this might be a design language, a complication focus, a material, a heritage narrative, or a consumer segment. Without differentiation, you are competing on price.
Watch: 
Baltic: vintage-inspired French design language at accessible price.
02  Collaborate
Brands are built by ecosystems. For a watch brand: your movement supplier, case manufacturer, retailer, press, and community all contribute to what your brand means. Choose collaborators who add to the brand's credibility.
Watch: 
AnOrdain collaborating with Scottish craftspeople for enamel dials.
03  Innovate
Differentiation must be actively maintained. As competitors catch up, you must evolve. In watches: new materials, new complications, new design directions — always in service of the core positioning.
Watch: 
Grand Seiko's Spring Drive caliber: a genuine mechanical innovation.
04  Validate
Test your ideas with real audiences before investing in production. For watches: early renders, community engagement (Reddit, forums), collaborations with reviewers. The watch community is vocal — use this.
Watch: 
Fratello's 'Building a Watch Brand' series validating VPC designs publicly.
05  Cultivate
Brand-building is a long-term activity. Consistency compounds. Every watch released, every Instagram post, every customer interaction is an investment — or a withdrawal — from brand equity.
Watch: 
Rolex's 70-year design consistency as the ultimate brand equity investment.

heading: Design as Competitive Advantage
original:
"Form follows emotion. Function follows form. And everything follows culture."
— Hartmut Esslinger, founder of Frog Design. Designed Apple's Snow White design language (1980s) that defined personal computing aesthetics for a decade.
Design as Differentiation
When products are functionally similar, design becomes the primary basis for choice. In the CHF 500–2,000 microbrand segment, almost every watch uses similar Swiss or Japanese movements. The watch that sells is the one whose design language most precisely addresses its target consumer.
Two watches, both ETA 2824, both 40mm. One sells at retail. One sits in inventory. The only difference is design quality and brand consistency.

Every design decision communicates a value. Polished bevels say 'craft matters.' A matte titanium case says 'function matters.' A guilloché dial says 'heritage matters.' These are not arbitrary choices — they are conversations with your target consumer. Understand what they value before you design.

Strong design creates barriers to imitation. If your watch looks like everything else, anyone can copy it. If your watch has a distinctive, coherent design language — Snowflake hands, Aquaracer-specific case proportions, AnOrdain enamel — copying it requires obvious plagiarism that damages the imitator's credibility.
Tudor's Snowflake hand is trademarked. The Grand Seiko Style is copyrighted. Design as IP protection is underexplored in the microbrand space.

heading: AnOrdain — When Craft Is the Brand
original:
The AnOrdain Model
Origin (Glasgow, 2015)
No Swiss heritage, no advertising, no distributor. The brand was built on one specific craft: hand-made enamel dials, a technique almost lost to the industry.
The dial is the brand
AnOrdain's enamel dials — made by their own artisans in Glasgow — are the entire differentiator. No two are identical. This creates scarcity, emotional connection, and a story impossible to copy at scale.
Price as integrity signal
Model 1 starts at £1,000. This is not arbitrary. At this price, the enamel craft is credible as a luxury statement. At £300, it would seem incongruous. Price communicates the seriousness of the craft.
Provenance and geography
Scottish-made watches carry no historical watch prestige — yet AnOrdain uses their Glasgow origin as a positive differentiator: independent, non-Swiss, authentically crafted in a specific place by identifiable people.
Critical recognition
Consistently featured by Hodinkee, Worn & Wound, and Fratello as a benchmark craft microbrand. AnOrdain's fumé enamel dials are cited industry-wide as proof that hand-craft and independent spirit can generate genuine collector desire without Swiss heritage or marketing spend.

heading: Swissness — What You Can and Cannot Claim
original:
The Swissness Act (in force since 2017) legally defines when a watch may use 'Swiss Made'. This is a brand positioning constraint, not optional knowledge.
SWISS MADE ✓
Movement assembled and inspected in Switzerland · At least 60% of production value from Switzerland · Technical development in Switzerland
Rolex, Omega, Patek, IWC, Nomos (German, cannot use this) — requires genuine Swiss manufacturing infrastructure.
SWISS MOVEMENT ✓
Movement is Swiss-made but assembly, casing, or other production occurs outside Switzerland · Cannot claim 'Swiss Made' on dial
Some microbrand models using Sellita or ETA movements but assembled in Hong Kong or China. Honest and legal.
NO SWISS CLAIM ✗
Japanese movement (Miyota, Seagull) or movement with under 60% Swiss value content · No Swiss manufacturing or development
Baltic (Miyota, Seagull), Lorier, most affordable microbrands. No Swiss claim can be made — even if the watch is well-designed.
⚠  Brand brief implication: If you cannot legally claim 'Swiss Made', do not position your brand as Swiss. The watch media and collector community will check.

The movement determines subdial positions. The designer works within — not around — these constraints.
ETA 7750 Chronograph
Layout: 
Subdials at 3 (30min), 6 (12hr), 9 (small seconds). Date at 4.

Creates a 3/6/9 subdial arrangement. Dial must be designed around these fixed positions. Many brands mask the 9 position.

Challenge:

heading: Water Resistance Standards
original:
One of the most misunderstood specifications — and a critical brand brief decision.
3 ATM / 30m
Splash Resistant
Protects against accidental splashes and rain only. Cannot be submerged. Do not wear swimming.
Design: 
Dress watches, fashion watches. No crown guards needed. Thin case possible. Most common on ultra-thin designs.
5 ATM / 50m
Light Water Contact
Brief submersion acceptable but not recommended for swimming. ISO 2281 standard.
Design: 
Most general-purpose watches. No screwdown crown required. Acceptable for most daily wear including washing hands.
10 ATM / 100m
Swimming
Suitable for swimming and snorkelling. Not diving. ISO 2281. Most lifestyle sports watches.
Design: 
Screwdown crown begins to appear. Case construction more robust. Tudor, lower Rolex, most quality sports watches.
20 ATM / 200m
Scuba Diving
ISO 6425 diving standard. Requires screwdown crown, unidirectional rotating bezel, luminous indices, anti-reflective crystal.
Design: 
The functional diver spec. Submariner, Fifty Fathoms, Pelagos. Case must accommodate gasket compression under pressure.
30 ATM / 300m+
Professional Diving
Saturation diving. ISO 6425 with extended depth rating. Helium escape valve in most cases.
Design: 
Rolex Sea-Dweller, Omega Ploprof, Seiko Marinemaster. Case walls significantly thicker. Very different design language.
⚠  Critical: ATM ratings are static pressure tests. Dynamic wrist movement creates higher pressure — a 3 ATM watch will leak in the swimming pool. Specify WR for your brand brief's intended use context, not marketing aspirations.

heading: Why Pencil Before Screen
original:
01
Speed of exploration
A rough sketch takes 2 minutes. A CAD model takes 2 hours. In the time it takes to model one idea badly, you can sketch 60 ideas roughly. The sketch phase is where you discover what you want to build — not where you build it.
02
Freedom from commitment
A sketch is disposable. When you're in CAD, every decision feels permanent — so you make fewer decisions. Sketching removes the fear of the wrong choice. Bad sketches are not waste; they are elimination of bad directions.
03
Physical intuition
Your hand knows things your brain doesn't yet. A proportion that looks right on paper, drawn quickly, is telling you something your analytical mind hasn't processed. Trust the sketch. Analyse it later.
04
Communication tool
Sketches communicate faster than words to collaborators, clients, and manufacturers. The Fratello 'Building a Watch Brand' series shows design sketches published the morning they were drawn — before any 3D model existed.

heading: Designing for the Wrist — Ergonomics
original:
A watch that looks elegant on a flat surface can sit uncomfortably on an actual wrist. Sketch and evaluate on wrist templates, not just dial-up views.
Lug Curvature
The wrist is curved (radius ~35mm). Straight lugs on a flat caseback will create a bridge — only touching at the case edges. Lugs must curve downward to follow the wrist. The tighter the curve, the more intimately the watch sits. No curve: the watch rocks uncomfortably.
Sketch tip: 
In your side-view sketch, draw the wrist profile as a gentle curve. The lug tips should meet the wrist, not float above it.
Lug-to-Lug vs Wrist Width
A lug-to-lug measurement exceeding the wearer's wrist width creates visual overhang on both sides. This reads as clunky even when the case diameter is appropriate. Typical wrist widths: 16–20cm circumference (male). Lug-to-lug ideally under 47mm for most wrists.
Sketch tip: 
When sketching, add the wrist silhouette in your front view. The lugs should not extend significantly beyond the wrist edges.
Case Back Curvature
A flat case back on a round case sits on its edge — uncomfortably high. A curved or shaped caseback follows the wrist contour and lowers the effective wearing height by 0.5–2mm. This is why Grand Seiko cases feel lower than their spec height suggests.
Sketch tip: 
In the side-view cross-section sketch, curve the caseback profile inward. Note that exhibition casebacks make curvature harder — flat glass requires a flat seating surface.
Crown Clearance
The crown protrudes from the 3 o'clock position. On a right-wrist wearer, this digs into the hand between thumb and forefinger. Crown guards (extensions of the case protecting the crown) prevent this. A screwdown crown sits lower and is less obtrusive.
Sketch tip: 
In the side view, draw the crown and check its clearance relationship with the simulated hand position. This is why diving watches have crown guards.

heading: Building a Watch Case in Vector
original:
01
Start with circles
Draw the outer case circle and inner bezel circle using the Ellipse tool. Set them concentric using Align panel. These establish case diameter and bezel width.
02
Construct lugs with Pen tool
Draw one lug shape carefully using bezier curves. Reflect vertically and horizontally to create all four matching lugs. Use Object → Transform → Reflect.
03
Dial circle and chapter ring
Draw the dial circle inside the bezel. Draw the chapter ring as a slightly smaller concentric circle. Use Pathfinder Minus Front to create the chapter ring as a stroked ring.
04
Hour markers
Create one index shape. Use Effect → Distort → Transform → Rotate with Copies to distribute all 12 markers at 30° intervals around the centre.
05
Hands
Draw the hour and minute hand along the 12 o'clock axis. Group them separately. The minute hand tip should reach the inner edge of the chapter ring precisely.
06
Crown
Draw the crown on the right side. Even in 2D front view, suggest the crown's cylindrical form with gradients.

heading: Dial Design & Typography
original:
The dial is typography. Treat every text element as a design decision.
Brand name typeface
Must align with brand DNA. Serif (traditional, luxury). Sans-serif (modern, technical). Never use decorative or display fonts — they read as amateur. Suggested starting points: Garamond, Optima, Futura, Helvetica Neue.
Size hierarchy
Brand name should be the largest text on the dial. Model name (if present) 50–70% of brand name height. 'Swiss Made' at the bottom: 40–50% of brand name. 'Automatic' text: same size as Swiss Made. Never make these elements compete.
Spacing and positioning
Brand name at 12 o'clock: very formal. At 6 o'clock: modern. Between 5–7: contemporary. Whatever you choose, maintain the same position across all models. Test legibility at watch scale (print 1:1).
Index typography
If using Arabic numerals: choose one typeface and stick to it. Lining figures (equal height numbers) read better at small sizes. Old-style figures (ascending/descending) feel classical. 12, 3, 6, 9 should visually anchor the dial.
'Swiss Made' requirement
For watches manufactured in Switzerland: legally required on the dial. For microbrands using Swiss movements but assembled elsewhere: do not falsely claim this. 'Swiss movement' is different from 'Swiss Made' — know the difference.

heading: Fusion 360 for Watch Designers
original:
The four operations you need to master before modelling a watch case.
Sketch + Extrude
Draw a 2D profile (your case outline) and push it into the third dimension. This is how every case body starts. The sketch is your precise 2D drawing brought into Fusion.
Tip: 
Set your sketch plane to top view. Sketch the case profile exactly matching your 2D orthographic.
Revolve
Rotate a profile around an axis. Used for rotationally symmetric elements: the crown, round case bodies, watch glass profiles.
Tip: 
A round case body can be modelled as a revolved profile — faster and more dimensionally accurate than a sketch+extrude approach.
Loft
Create a smooth transition between two different profiles. Essential for lug geometry — the lug cross-section at the case is different from the lug tip.
Tip: 
Create two sketch profiles (at case attachment and at lug tip) and loft between them. Control the transition with guide rails for smooth curves.
Fillet
Round sharp edges. Apply last — after all primary geometry is complete. The fillet radius is a major design element: large fillets feel soft/approachable, small fillets feel crisp/technical.
Tip: 
Never apply fillets during early modelling — they prevent later modifications. Build sharp geometry first, fillet in the final pass.

heading: The Case Modelling Sequence
original:
1
Import 2D orthographic as reference
File → Insert → Insert SVG or Sketch. Import your front view and side view as canvas backgrounds. Lock them. All geometry must align with these references.
2
Model the case body
Sketch the side profile of the case (top-view silhouette). Extrude or Revolve to the case height dimension. Result: a simple cylindrical or shaped case disc.
3
Cut the movement cavity
Sketch the movement cavity diameter and depth on the back face. Extrude-cut to the correct depth (movement height + 0.2mm clearance). This is the most dimensionally critical step.
4
Model the bezel
The bezel sits on top of the case body. For a round watch: offset the top face outward by bezel thickness. For sapphire crystal: model the crystal channel (a 0.5mm shelf inside the bezel).
5
Model the lugs
This is the hardest step. Create the lug cross-section as two sketches (at case end and at lug tip). Loft between them. Use a guide rail that follows your 2D side-view lug profile.
6
Crown hole and crown
Place the crown stem hole at the exact stem position from your spec sheet. Model the crown separately as a revolved profile. This tests whether your crown position was correctly specified.

heading: Surface Finishing — The Designer's Vocabulary
original:
Mirror Polish
Flat, highly reflective surface produced by progressively finer abrasives. The hallmark of Swiss finishing. Visible quality signal — any deviation shows. Requires perfectly flat surfaces (Zaratsu/Sallaz technique for distortion-free result).
→  
Rolex case flanks, dress watch bezels, applied hour markers
Brushed / Satin
Directional parallel scratches create a matte-directional surface. Less expensive than mirror polish. Can be applied in different directions on different case surfaces to create contrast.
→  
Standard sports watch case surfaces, titanium watches, field watches
Sandblasted / Bead-blasted
Uniform matte surface from abrasive media. No directional character. Clean, modern, technical. Popular in military-inspired and field watches. Very forgiving to produce.
→  
Tudor Black Bay Bronze caseback area, many field watches
Côtes de Genève (Geneva Stripes)
Parallel wave pattern applied to movement plates and bridges (and occasionally dial). Not a case finishing — a movement finishing. Signals quality when visible through exhibition caseback.
→  
Virtually all Swiss movement finishing, Grand Seiko movement plates
Perlage
Circular scratch pattern (like fish scales) applied to movement parts not visible in use. Part of haute horlogerie finishing standard even for invisible surfaces.
→  
Traditional Swiss finishing — Patek, AP, FP Journe movement components
PVD / DLC Coating
Physical Vapour Deposition. Deposits a very hard layer (black, gold, bronze colour) onto the case. Highly scratch resistant but uniform — loses the polish/brushed contrast that makes uncoated cases beautiful.
→  
Black case sports watches, tactical watches. AP Royal Oak Offshore black.

heading: Swissness Act & Crystal Specification
original:
The Swissness Act (in force 2017)
What it controls
Who may legally use 'Swiss Made' on a watch dial
60% rule
At least 60% of the total value of the watch's components must be of Swiss origin
Movement requirement
Movement must be Swiss: assembled and inspected in Switzerland with Swiss components
Development in CH
Technical development of the watch must have occurred in Switzerland
'Swiss Movement'
A weaker claim — means only the movement is Swiss; the watch case may be from anywhere
Penalties
Using 'Swiss Made' without qualifying: criminal offence under Swiss law, EU unfair competition
Crystal Specification
Sapphire (single AR)
One layer anti-reflective coating. Standard for most mid-tier watches. Significantly reduces glare vs uncoated.
Sapphire (double AR)
Both internal and external surfaces coated. Best clarity. Standard for serious watches CHF 500+. Specify this.
Domed vs flat
Domed sapphire (box crystal): vintage aesthetic, distortion at edges, dramatic in person. Flat: modern, cleaner renders.
Hesalite (acrylic)
Baltic's signature crystal choice. Lighter, softer, but polishes out scratches. Creates warm vintage haze. Intentional choice.
Mineral glass
Harder than acrylic, cheaper than sapphire. Mid-tier budget option. Not appropriate above ~CHF 400 positioning.

heading: The Watch as a Colour System
original:
Dial colour is one element. Every layer of the watch participates in a colour conversation.
Case Metal
Sets the tonal key: silver (steel/titanium), warm grey (bronze), gold (yellow/rose/white). Everything else responds to this.
→  
Warm case → warm dial. Cool case → cool or neutral dial.
Dial Colour
Primary visual statement. Interacts with case metal through the apertures, indices, and any cutaway elements.
→  
Test at multiple light temperatures — sunburst dials shift most dramatically.
Index Metal
Applied gold on steel: cross-metal contrast, formal. Steel on steel: monochromatic, modern. Gold on gold: tonal.
→  
Index metal often inverts case metal. Both approaches are valid if intentional.
Lume Grade
BGW9 (blue-white) on warm dial: deliberate tension. C3 (yellow-green) on black: maximum legibility. C1 (cream) on champagne: tonal harmony.
→  
Lume colour is part of the system — specify it as such.
Strap/Bracelet
~50% of visible surface area. Leather grain and colour, rubber tone, bracelet metal and finish — all extend the colour language onto the wrist.
→  
Complete the system, don't compete with it. Specify multiple options — buyers choose.

heading: KeyShot Workflow for Watches
original:
01
Import from Fusion 360
File → Import. KeyShot accepts .step, .iges, .obj, .fbx. The .step from Fusion 360 imports best — preserves material groups if set up correctly in Fusion. Each component imports as a separate material group.
02
Set up HDRI environment
Environment tab. Start with a studio HDRI (neutral grey walls, soft diffused light). For watch renders specifically: start with 'Product Lighting' presets. Rotate the HDRI to find the best default light angle.
03
Assign materials from callout sheet
Drag materials from the library onto each part. Your Assignment 7 callout sheet is your guide. Polished metal goes on polished parts. Brushed metal on brushed surfaces. Pay attention to anisotropy direction on brushed parts.
04
HDRI pin editing (the key skill)
Open HDRI editor. Place a bright 'key' pin to create the main catch light on polished surfaces. Place a large soft fill pin opposite. For watches: the catch light on the dial and bezel is the most important element to nail.
05
Camera setup
Distance: 100–200mm focal length equivalent. This reduces distortion. Angle: 3/4 view at 45° above horizontal for most hero shots. Avoid straight-on front view for hero renders — it flattens the watch.
06
Render settings
For final renders: 300+ samples, max 3840×2160 (4K). For test renders: 50 samples, 1920×1080. Background: white (80% grey, not pure white) for portfolio. Black for editorial. Transparent for mockups.

heading: Building Your Portfolio Presentation
original:
The portfolio case study is how designers get work. It must tell a story, not just show results.
01
The Problem / Opportunity
What gap in the market or consumer need motivated this brand? Why does this watch need to exist? This is the strategic frame that makes everything that follows make sense.
02
The Consumer
Who is the target buyer? What motivates their purchase? Show that you understand people, not just products. One slide, one person, described specifically.
03
Design Process
Show the journey: brand brief → positioning map → concept sketches → 2D render evolution → 3D modelling → final renders. Process communicates design thinking — more valuable than results alone.
04
Design Rationale
For each major design decision (case shape, dial, finishing), one clear statement of why: 'The cushion case was chosen because... The fumé dial was avoided because...' Rationale is what separates design from decoration.
05
The Final Object
Hero renders. Maximum 4–6. Let the renders breathe. White space is not wasted space. One great render is more powerful than 12 average ones.
06
Technical Specification
The spec page. Demonstrates that this is a buildable product, not just a concept. Communicates professionalism and manufacturing awareness.

heading: Career Pathways in Watch Design
original:
Four Pathways into Watch Design
In-House Brand Designer
Entry: 
Industrial design degree. Strong portfolio including watch design. These roles are rare — most major brands have very small design teams (2–8 people).
Reality: 
High stability. Limited creative freedom. Design decisions go through multiple approval layers. The watch you design may take 3 years to reach market.
Independent/Freelance Designer
Entry: 
Portfolio of self-initiated work (exactly what this curriculum produces). Max Resnick model — build a portfolio, establish credibility through press and community.
Reality: 
High creative freedom. Variable income. Client acquisition requires networking. The most available pathway for self-taught designers.
Microbrand Founder
Entry: 
This curriculum provides the design foundation. Additional requirements: business model, manufacturer relationships, capital (~£30,000+ for first run), community building.
Reality: 
Highest risk, highest creative ownership. 500+ active microbrands — differentiation is survival. 90% fail within 5 years. Fratello's 'Building a Watch Brand' series is essential reading.
Watchmaking School → Design
Entry: 
Formal watchmaking training gives mechanical credibility that no design course can replace. Some watch designers (e.g. Kari Voutilainen) are trained watchmakers first.
Reality: 
The most rigorous pathway. 2–4 years of intensive training. Produces designers who understand movements at a physical level that completely changes design decision-making.

heading: Intellectual Property — What You Can and Cannot Own
original:
Designers navigate IP constantly. Knowing the basics prevents expensive mistakes — and teaches you to create designs worth protecting.
Trademark
Brand name, logo, distinctive phrases, sometimes colour (Tiffany blue). Registered per class and territory.
Watch context: 
Your brand name and logo should be trademarked. In the UK: UKIPO (£170 per class). In EU: EUIPO (€850 for one class). Search before naming — watch companies aggressively protect marks.
✓ Register your brand name and logo. ✗ Cannot trademark a generic case shape or a colour alone without extensive use.
Registered Design
The specific visual appearance of a product — its shape, configuration, surface ornamentation. Registered nationally or via Hague System.
Watch context: 
A distinctive case profile, bezel shape, or bracelet link design can be registered. Costs: ~£50–200 per design in the UK. Protects for up to 25 years.
✓ Register distinctive case and dial designs before launch. ✗ Cannot register a functional feature (e.g. a screwdown crown — that is a mechanism, not a design).
Copyright
Automatically applies to original creative works — dial artwork, hand designs, case drawings. No registration required in the UK/EU.
Watch context: 
Your sketches, renders, and technical drawings are automatically copyrighted from the moment of creation. Keep dated files. This prevents wholesale copying of your visual work.
✓ Automatic — but document your work with dated files. ✗ Cannot copyright a functional watch component or a design idea, only its specific expression.
Patent
Protects novel mechanical inventions. Expensive (~£5,000–20,000+ per territory) and requires genuine novelty.
Watch context: 
Only relevant if you have developed a genuinely new mechanism, movement component, or case feature. Not relevant for most microbrands — and attempting to patent existing mechanisms is invalid.
✗ Most microbrand designs do not meet the novelty threshold. Focus on trademark and registered design instead.

heading: Enamel Dial Techniques
original:
Enamel Dial Techniques — The Highest Craft
Grand Feu Enamel
Vitreous enamel fired at 800°C+. Multiple firings build depth and luminosity impossible to achieve with paint or printing. The most labour-intensive dial technique. AnOrdain's core technique. Each dial takes many hours and cannot be mass-produced.
Use when: 
For brands positioned above £1,000 with a craft narrative. Minimum cost impact: +£150–300 per dial from specialist supplier.
Fumé / Gradient
Achieved with Grand Feu enamel by controlling the firing temperature and time, or with vacuum deposition techniques for industrial versions. The gradient is the result of differential firing across the dial surface.
Use when: 
Currently trendy but proven — AnOrdain, H. Moser Cie., Baltic (printed version). The enamel version has depth; the printed version is flat.
Cloisonné
Enamel separated by fine gold or silver wires (cloisons) into compartments. Allows multi-colour designs with precise boundaries. Extremely time-consuming. Patek, Jaeger-LeCoultre use for ultra-luxury editions.
Use when: 
Only viable for ultra-high-end limited editions. Not relevant for microbrand design except as inspiration for printed dial patterns.
Guilloché + Enamel
Engine-turning (guilloché) creates a geometric pattern in the gold dial base, then translucent enamel is applied over it. The light interacts with the pattern through the enamel, creating depth unavailable any other way.
Use when: 
The hallmark of Breguet dials. Requires both a guilloché artist and an enamel specialist. Patek Philippe Calatrava, George Daniels watches.

heading: Independent Watchmaking
original:
The independent movement: F.P. Journe, De Bethune, Laurent Ferrier, Voutilainen, Gronefeld
F.P. Journe
Design: 
Restrained classical elegance. Brass movements, natural colour. Time-only purity. Tourbillons that are displayed functionally not decoratively. No sapphire crystal until recently.
Lesson: 
Design restraint as luxury signifier. When everything else competes for visual attention, radical simplicity reads as confidence.
De Bethune
Design: 
Future-forward interpretations of Swiss tradition. Spherical moon phase. Titanium and gold combinations. Polished steel with laser-frosted elements creating distinctive two-tone character.
Lesson: 
Materials innovation as design language. De Bethune develops proprietary alloys (DB25 titanium-gold) and uses a combination of traditional côtes de Genève, perlage, and mirror-polished bevels on movements. Their blue-tinted steel is achieved through controlled oxidation. The design work is inseparable from the materials research.
Kari Voutilainen
Design: 
Master of the traditional Finnish-Swiss aesthetic. Exceptional movement finishing visible through exhibition casebacks. Dials with extraordinary depth from multiple layers of lacquer and printing.
Lesson: 
Finishing quality as competitive strategy. Voutilainen watches are compared to Lange and Patek at half the price because every surface is exceptional.
MB&F
Design: 
Conceptual, sculptural, anti-conventional. Each piece is explicitly a 'horological machine' not a 'watch'. Collaborations with other independent watchmakers.
Lesson: 
Brand as creative philosophy. MB&F is defined by what it refuses to be (conventional, compromising, conservative) more than by what it makes. The most explicitly brand-driven of all independents.

Future-forward interpretations of Swiss tradition. Spherical moon phase. Titanium and gold combinations. Polished steel with laser-frosted elements creating distinctive two-tone character.

Materials innovation as design language. De Bethune develops proprietary alloys (DB25 titanium-gold) and uses a combination of traditional côtes de Genève, perlage, and mirror-polished bevels on movements. Their blue-tinted steel is achieved through controlled oxidation. The design work is inseparable from the materials research.
Master of the traditional Finnish-Swiss aesthetic. Exceptional movement finishing visible through exhibition casebacks. Dials with extraordinary depth from multiple layers of lacquer and printing.
Finishing quality as competitive strategy. Voutilainen watches are compared to Lange and Patek at half the price because every surface is exceptional.
Conceptual, sculptural, anti-conventional. Each piece is explicitly a 'horological machine' not a 'watch'. Collaborations with other independent watchmakers.
Brand as creative philosophy. MB&F is defined by what it refuses to be (conventional, compromising, conservative) more than by what it makes. The most explicitly brand-driven of all independents.

heading: Continuing Your Education
original:
WOSTEP Programme
The world's premier watchmaking school. Understanding how to make a watch at a technical level transforms how you design them. 1,800-hour or 3,000-hour programmes. British School of Watchmaking in Manchester offers UK access.
wostep.ch
GrabCAD Reverse Engineering
Download professional watch CAD models. Spend one hour per week studying how experienced engineers build case geometry, handle tolerances, and design for manufacturing. Free.
grabcad.com/library/tag/watch
Auction House Deep Dives
Christie's and Sotheby's watch auction catalogues are free and contain the most detailed photography of movements and dials available anywhere. Study 3–5 lots per week as visual research.
christies.com/watches
Watches & Wonders Annual
The premier watch fair. Even if not attending: study every press release as brand strategy research. Identify design decisions. Ask 'Why did they make this choice now?'
watchesandwonders.com
Language Learning
French and German open the primary source literature in horology (most significant historical texts, manufacturer archives, and technical documentation). Even basic reading ability is valuable.
Duolingo for conversational, then historical texts
